conflicts.name: Constantine at the Milvian Bridge and the Christian empire's wars
conflicts.region: Italy, the Balkans and the Bosporus (Roman Empire)
conflicts.religionRoleNote: These were Roman civil wars for supreme power between rival emperors of the Tetrarchy, and would have been fought whatever the gods of the contenders. Religion entered because Constantine attributed his victory of 312 to the God of the Christians and fought under a Christian sign, and because Christian writers, above all Eusebius of Caesarea, presented his final war against Licinius in 324 as the defeat of a persecutor. Historians have long debated Constantine's sincerity: Jacob Burckhardt saw a calculating politician, while Timothy Barnes and others argue for a real if theologically unsophisticated conversion around 312. Most now accept that he genuinely believed the Christian God gave victory, but that the wars themselves were dynastic and political; religion supplied legitimacy and a new language of divinely sanctioned battle rather than the cause.

sides.name: Constantine (Augustus in the West, from 324 sole emperor)
sides.faith: Favoured Christianity from 312; earlier a devotee of Sol Invictus

sides.name: Maxentius (ruler of Rome and Italy, 306–312)
sides.faith: Traditional Roman religion; tolerant of Christians in Italy

sides.name: Licinius (Augustus in the East, 308–324)
sides.faith: Traditional Roman religion; co-author of the 313 settlement, later restricted Christians

conflicts.summary: Between 312 and 324 Constantine fought his way from Gaul to sole rule of the Roman world, first defeating Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome after, by his own later account, seeing a sign in the sky and being told 'in this sign conquer', and finally overthrowing his eastern colleague Licinius at Adrianople and Chrysopolis. The wars were struggles for imperial power, but they created the first Christian emperor and the first Christian theology of victory in battle.
conflicts.story:
By 306 the system of four co-emperors created by Diocletian had collapsed into rivalry. Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his father's troops at York; Maxentius, son of the retired emperor Maximian, seized Rome. At the same time the Great Persecution of Christians, begun in 303, was ending unevenly: Galerius issued an edict of toleration in 311, but persecution continued for a while in the East under Maximinus Daia. Christians thus had strong reasons to watch the emperors' contest closely.

In spring 312 Constantine crossed the Alps from Gaul with a relatively small army, perhaps forty thousand men, took Segusio (Susa), defeated Maxentius' heavy cavalry near Turin, captured Milan, and won a hard battle at Verona, where Maxentius' praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus was killed. He then marched on Rome. Maxentius, who had prepared the city for a siege, unexpectedly came out to fight and drew up his army with the Tiber at its back near the Milvian Bridge.

The religious tradition about the battle comes from two Christian authors who knew Constantine. Lactantius, writing about 314–315, says Constantine was told in a dream to mark 'the heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields, a Chi-Rho or staurogram. Eusebius, in his Life of Constantine written after the emperor's death in 337, reports the emperor's own sworn account of a cross of light seen in the sky with the words 'by this conquer' (in Greek, touto nika; in Latin tradition, in hoc signo vinces), followed by a dream in which Christ told him to make a standard of the sign, the labarum. On 28 October 312 Maxentius' army broke; the retreat across a temporary bridge of boats collapsed and Maxentius drowned in the Tiber. Constantine entered Rome, had Maxentius' head paraded on a spear, and dissolved the praetorian guard.

Early in 313 Constantine and Licinius met at Milan and agreed the policy of religious freedom and restitution of Christian property usually called the Edict of Milan. Licinius then defeated Maximinus Daia, who had resumed persecution, near Adrianople; Lactantius claims Licinius' soldiers recited a prayer to the 'Supreme God' given by an angel. The two victors soon fell out. A first war in 316–317 brought battles at Cibalae and Mardia and gave Constantine most of the Balkans. Over the following years Licinius, suspecting Christians of loyalty to his rival, expelled them from his household and army, restricted church synods and was accused of further harassment.

In 324 Constantine attacked again, now presenting himself as protector of Christians in the East. He defeated Licinius at Adrianople on 3 July; his son Crispus destroyed Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont; and on 18 September Constantine won the decisive battle of Chrysopolis on the Asian shore of the Bosporus. Eusebius describes the labarum carried before the army, a tent of prayer in the camp and priests accompanying the troops. Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia after his wife Constantia, Constantine's sister, pleaded for his life; he was promised safety but was executed at Thessalonica in 325, as was his young son a little later.

As sole emperor Constantine summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325 and founded Constantinople, dedicated in 330, on the site of the old Byzantium near the scene of his final victory. Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History and Life of Constantine framed the whole sequence as God's deliverance of his church through a chosen emperor, a reading that shaped Christian political thought for more than a thousand years and made the cross a military emblem.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Constantine's soldiers fought under the Chi-Rho painted on their shields (Lactantius) and behind the labarum, a jewelled standard bearing the Chi-Rho, which Eusebius says had power to give victory and was guarded by a special detachment. The vision's message, 'by this conquer' (in hoc signo vinces), became the classic formula of the cross as a sign of victory. Eusebius portrayed Licinius as a new Pharaoh and Constantine as a new Moses, and described prayers in a portable tabernacle before battle. The triumphal Arch of Constantine (315) diplomatically credits victory to 'the inspiration of the divinity' (instinctu divinitatis) without naming Christ.
religiousCauses: Constantine's belief, from 312, that the God of the Christians had granted him victory and would continue to do so if properly honoured.
The recent Great Persecution (303–311/313) gave Christians, and Constantine's propaganda, an interest in which emperors would protect or persecute the church.
Licinius' later restrictions on Christians allowed Constantine to frame the war of 324 as the liberation of eastern Christians from a persecutor.
Eusebius' providential theology, in which the emperor is God's agent on earth, gave the wars a sacred meaning after the event.
otherCauses: The breakdown of the Tetrarchy after Diocletian's abdication in 305 left several men with armies and claims to the purple.
Constantine's personal ambition and dynastic claim as son of Constantius I, and his wish to unite the empire under one ruler and his sons.
Control of Rome, Italy and the wealthy eastern provinces, with their tax revenues and armies.
Mutual suspicion and broken agreements between Constantine and Licinius after 313, including disputes over Caesars appointed for their sons.
triggers: Maxentius' declaration of war on Constantine, ostensibly to avenge his father Maximian, gave Constantine the occasion to invade Italy in 312.
The elevation of Bassianus and a disputed plot in 316 led to the first war between Constantine and Licinius.
Constantine's pursuit of Sarmatian and Gothic raiders into Licinius' territory in 323 provoked the final war of 324.

timeline.text: Diocletian launches the Great Persecution of Christians.
Constantine proclaimed emperor at York; Maxentius seizes Rome.
Galerius' edict of toleration ends persecution in much of the empire.
Constantine invades Italy, wins at Turin and Verona, and defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October.
Constantine and Licinius agree the 'Edict of Milan'; Licinius defeats Maximinus Daia.
The Arch of Constantine is dedicated in Rome, crediting victory to the 'divinity'.
First war between Constantine and Licinius: battles of Cibalae and Mardia (316–317).
Licinius begins to purge Christians from his court and army and restrict church synods.
Constantine defeats Licinius at Adrianople (July), at sea in the Hellespont, and at Chrysopolis (18 September).
Licinius executed at Thessalonica; Constantine summons the Council of Nicaea.
Constantinople dedicated near the site of the final victory.

keyPeople.name: Constantine I
keyPeople.focus: Invaded Italy in 312, fought under the Chi-Rho at the Milvian Bridge, and defeated Licinius in 316–317 and 324.
keyPeople.outcome: Sole emperor from 324; patron of the church, convener of Nicaea, baptised on his deathbed in 337 and venerated as a saint in the East.

keyPeople.name: Maxentius
keyPeople.focus: Held Rome against Constantine; came out to fight at the Milvian Bridge.
keyPeople.outcome: Drowned in the Tiber during the rout; his memory was condemned and he was later depicted as a tyrant.

keyPeople.name: Licinius
keyPeople.focus: Ally of Constantine in 313, then his rival in two wars; later restricted Christians in his domains.
keyPeople.outcome: Defeated at Chrysopolis, surrendered at Nicomedia and executed in 325 despite a promise of safety.

keyPeople.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
keyPeople.focus: Recorded Constantine's account of the vision and interpreted the wars as God's deliverance of the church.
keyPeople.outcome: His Ecclesiastical History and Life of Constantine founded the Christian imperial ideal of the 'Christian emperor'.

keyPeople.name: Lactantius
keyPeople.role: Christian rhetorician and tutor to Constantine's son Crispus
keyPeople.focus: Earliest source for the dream and the heavenly sign on the shields in On the Deaths of the Persecutors.
keyPeople.outcome: His work is the main near-contemporary Christian narrative of the persecutions and civil wars.

keyPeople.name: Crispus
keyPeople.focus: Destroyed Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont in 324.
keyPeople.outcome: Executed on his father's orders in 326 for reasons never explained.

casualties.note: No credible figures survive for losses at Turin, Verona, the Milvian Bridge, Cibalae, Adrianople or Chrysopolis; ancient numbers for army sizes (for example Zosimus' claim of very large forces at Chrysopolis) are generally regarded as exaggerated, so no estimate range is given.

effects: Constantine became master of the West in 312 and of the whole empire in 324, ending the Tetrarchy.
The church gained legal security, restored property and growing imperial patronage after 313.
A new capital, Constantinople, was founded near the site of the final victory.
The cross and Chi-Rho became imperial and military emblems, carried on standards for centuries.
Emperors began to intervene directly in church disputes, starting with the Donatist controversy and Nicaea.
effectsOnChurch: Christianity moved from a persecuted minority to an imperially favoured religion within a decade.
Eusebius' theology of the Christian emperor as God's vice-regent shaped Byzantine and later Western political theology.
The earlier strong Christian reluctance about military service weakened; the Council of Arles (314) penalised soldiers who threw down their arms in peacetime.
The association of the cross with military victory laid foundations for later ideas of holy war, though not yet for crusade.
conflicts.legacy: The Milvian Bridge became one of the hinges of Christian history: the beginning of 'Constantinian' Christianity, praised by Eusebius and much of the later church as providential and criticised by Anabaptists, many modern theologians and historians of Christian pacifism as the moment the church accepted the sword. The phrase 'in this sign conquer' was later used by crusaders, monarchies and military orders. Historians continue to debate what Constantine saw, perhaps a solar halo phenomenon, and how far his conversion shaped his policies.

dissenters.name: Lactantius (earlier writings)
dissenters.text: In his Divine Institutes (c. 303–311), written before he became a court writer, Lactantius taught that a just man may not serve as a soldier and that killing a human being is always wrong, a view that sat uneasily with his later celebration of Constantine's victories.

dissenters.name: Martin of Tours
dissenters.text: A generation later, in 356, Martin, then serving in the army of Constantine's son Constantius II under the Caesar Julian, reportedly refused a donative before battle saying 'I am a soldier of Christ; it is not lawful for me to fight' (Sulpicius Severus, Life of Martin), showing that the older Christian reluctance about war survived within the Christian empire.

dissenters.name: Christian pacifist tradition (Tertullian, Origen)
dissenters.text: Pre-Constantinian writers such as Tertullian and Origen had argued that Christians should not shed blood in war; their views were remembered, though increasingly marginal, after 312.

theatres.name: Battle of the Milvian Bridge (Saxa Rubra)

campaigns.title: Constantine's invasion of Italy, 312
campaigns.people: Constantine and his Gallic and Rhine army
campaigns.text: Crossing the Alps by the Mont Cenis route, Constantine took Susa, beat Maxentius' cavalry at Turin, was welcomed at Milan, broke the northern army at Verona and marched down the Via Flaminia to the Tiber, where Maxentius was defeated and drowned on 28 October.

campaigns.title: The final war against Licinius, 324
campaigns.people: Constantine, with Crispus commanding the fleet
campaigns.text: From his base at Thessalonica Constantine advanced into Thrace, won at Adrianople on 3 July, besieged Byzantium while Crispus cleared the Hellespont, crossed to Asia and won the decisive battle of Chrysopolis on 18 September; Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia.

conflicts.name: Heraclius' war with Persia and the True Cross
conflicts.region: Eastern Roman (Byzantine) and Sasanian Persian empires: Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, the Caucasus and Mesopotamia
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The war began as a great-power conflict: Khosrow II invaded in 603 claiming to avenge his patron, the murdered emperor Maurice, and the stakes were territory, tribute and survival. Religion became major after the Persian capture of Jerusalem in 614 and the removal of the relic of the True Cross to Ctesiphon. Heraclius' counter-offensives of 622–628 were accompanied by icons, sermons and the destruction of Zoroastrian fire temples, and his return of the Cross to Jerusalem in 630 was celebrated as a religious triumph. Some historians have called this the 'first crusade'; Walter Kaegi and James Howard-Johnston are more cautious, stressing Heraclius' strategic brilliance and diplomacy and noting that much of the religious colouring comes from later chroniclers such as Theophanes and from court poetry. The Persian side was not waging a religious war against Christianity as such: Khosrow had Christian wives and advisers and many of his subjects belonged to the Church of the East.

sides.name: Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire
sides.faith: Chalcedonian Christianity, with large Miaphysite populations in Syria and Egypt

sides.name: Sasanian Persian Empire
sides.faith: Zoroastrianism (state religion), with large Christian (Church of the East and Miaphysite) and Jewish minorities

conflicts.summary: The last and greatest war between Rome and Persia lasted a quarter of a century. Persian armies overran Syria, Palestine and Egypt, took Jerusalem in 614 and carried off the True Cross, and with the Avars besieged Constantinople in 626. Heraclius turned the war around with bold campaigns through Armenia and the Caucasus, destroyed the great Zoroastrian fire temple at Ganzak, crushed a Persian army near Nineveh in 627 and forced a peace in 628. He returned the Cross to Jerusalem in 630, only for both exhausted empires to face the Arab conquests within a few years.
conflicts.story:
In 602 the emperor Maurice, who had restored Khosrow II to the Persian throne in 591, was overthrown and murdered with his sons by the centurion Phocas. Khosrow declared war in 603, claiming to avenge his benefactor, and paraded a pretender said to be Maurice's son. Phocas' unpopular regime struggled; Persian armies took the Roman fortress of Dara in 604 and pushed into Armenia and Anatolia. In 610 Heraclius, son of the exarch of Carthage, sailed from Africa, overthrew and executed Phocas, and became emperor, but for years he could not stop the Persian advance.

The Persians took Antioch in 613 and Damascus soon after. In spring 614 the general Shahrbaraz besieged Jerusalem; after about three weeks the walls were breached. The monk Strategius, an eyewitness, describes days of slaughter of Christians, the burning of churches including the Holy Sepulchre, and the deportation of the patriarch Zacharias and many captives to Persia, together with the relic of the True Cross. Local Jews, who had suffered under Christian rule and had been briefly allowed to govern the city by the Persians, were blamed by Christian writers for part of the killing; the scale of the massacre in Strategius' figures is not trusted, but excavated mass burials in Jerusalem confirm heavy loss of life. Egypt, the empire's granary, fell between 618 and 621, and a Persian army camped at Chalcedon within sight of Constantinople.

Heraclius gave the struggle a sacred character. With the church's consent he melted down church plate to pay his troops, and in 622 he left the capital carrying an icon of Christ 'not made by human hands', addressing his army as men fighting for God and for the captive Christians. In campaigns of 622–625 he manoeuvred through Anatolia and Armenia, and in 623 or 624 he sacked Ganzak and destroyed the great fire temple of Adur Gushnasp at Takht-i Suleiman in retaliation for Jerusalem. He wintered in Albania (in the Caucasus) and allied with the Western Turks, who ravaged Persian territory and besieged Tiflis.

In the summer of 626, while Heraclius remained in the East, a huge Avar and Slav host besieged Constantinople from the European side as a Persian army under Shahrbaraz waited across the Bosporus. The patriarch Sergius led processions with the icon of the Virgin round the walls, and when the Avar assault and the Slav canoe fleet failed in early August the defenders attributed their deliverance to the Theotokos; the hymn known as the Akathist became associated with the victory. Heraclius' brother Theodore defeated another Persian army in Anatolia.

In autumn 627 Heraclius invaded Mesopotamia from the Caucasus with Turkic support. On 12 December he defeated the Persian army under Rhahzadh near the ruins of Nineveh, killing its commander in single combat according to the chronicles. He went on to sack Khosrow's palace at Dastagird. Khosrow's authority collapsed: in February 628 he was deposed and murdered by his son Kavad II (Shiroe), who made peace on the basis of the old frontiers, prisoners released and the Cross returned. Persia then fell into civil war, with several rulers in four years.

After negotiations with Shahrbaraz, who briefly seized the Persian throne, the relic of the Cross was restored. Heraclius brought it into Jerusalem in a solemn procession, traditionally on 21 March 630, the origin of the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross associated with his name in the West. The victory was followed by reprisals: Jews were expelled from Jerusalem and many killed, and in 632 Heraclius ordered the forced baptism of Jews in the empire. In the same years he and Patriarch Sergius sought to reunite Miaphysite Christians through the formulas of Monoenergism and later Monothelitism, which caused new division. Within a decade of the triumph Arab Muslim armies, facing two drained empires, took Syria, Palestine and Egypt from Byzantium (Yarmuk 636, Jerusalem 637/638) and destroyed the Sasanian state.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Heraclius' campaigns were framed as a war for Christ and the captive Cross. He carried the icon of Christ 'not made by hands' (the acheiropoietos image), was praised by the court poet George of Pisidia as a new David and Heraclius-Hercules fighting the fire-worshippers, and according to Theophanes urged his soldiers to win the crown of martyrdom. The destruction of the Zoroastrian fire temple at Ganzak was presented as revenge for the burning of Jerusalem. In Constantinople in 626 Patriarch Sergius processed the icons of Christ and the Virgin round the walls, and victory was credited to the Theotokos. The restoration of the True Cross to Jerusalem in 630 was a deliberate religious ceremony of triumph.
religiousCauses: The capture of Jerusalem in 614, the burning of churches and the removal of the True Cross to Persia gave the war a sacred cause for Roman Christians.
Byzantine imperial ideology held the emperor to be the protector of Christendom and of the holy places.
Christian–Jewish tensions in Palestine shaped the violence of 614 and the reprisals of 629–632.
Sasanian kings used Zoroastrian kingship ideology, and fire temples were symbolic targets for Heraclius.
otherCauses: Centuries of Roman–Persian rivalry over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the frontier fortresses.
Khosrow II's opportunistic claim to avenge Maurice after Phocas' coup of 602.
Internal Byzantine instability under Phocas and civil war in 608–610 that weakened the eastern defences.
The ambitions of Khosrow II to restore the Achaemenid empire's boundaries, and the wealth of Syria and Egypt.
Steppe politics: the Avars' pressure on the Balkans and the Western Turks' readiness to ally with Constantinople.
triggers: The murder of the emperor Maurice and his sons by Phocas in November 602.
The Persian capture of Jerusalem and the True Cross in 614, which transformed the war's meaning for Christians.
Heraclius' departure from Constantinople on campaign at Easter 622.

timeline.text: Phocas overthrows and murders Maurice.
Khosrow II declares war to avenge Maurice.
Heraclius overthrows Phocas and becomes emperor.
Persians defeat Heraclius near Antioch and take the city.
Shahrbaraz captures Jerusalem; massacre, burning of churches and deportation of the True Cross.
Persian conquest of Egypt; Alexandria falls (c. 619).
Heraclius launches his counter-offensive in Anatolia with the icon of Christ.
Heraclius sacks Ganzak and destroys the fire temple at Takht-i Suleiman.
Avar–Persian siege of Constantinople fails in August.
Heraclius and Turkic allies besiege Tiflis; victory near Nineveh on 12 December.
Khosrow II deposed and killed; Kavad II makes peace.
Heraclius restores the True Cross to Jerusalem (traditionally 21 March).
Heraclius orders the forced baptism of Jews.
Arab Muslim victory at the Yarmuk ends Byzantine rule in Syria.

keyPeople.name: Heraclius
keyPeople.origin: Son of the exarch of Africa, Carthage
keyPeople.focus: Rebuilt the army, led the campaigns of 622–628 in person and restored the True Cross.
keyPeople.outcome: Hailed as a saviour, he lived to see Syria, Palestine and Egypt lost to the Arabs; his religious union policies split the church.

keyPeople.name: Khosrow II
keyPeople.focus: Launched the war in 603 and conquered the Roman East.
keyPeople.outcome: Deposed and executed by his son Kavad II after the defeat at Nineveh.

keyPeople.name: Sergius of Constantinople
keyPeople.focus: Lent church treasure for the war and led the religious defence of Constantinople during the siege of 626.
keyPeople.outcome: Architect of Monoenergism and the Ekthesis (638); later condemned as a Monothelite at the Third Council of Constantinople.

keyPeople.name: Shahrbaraz
keyPeople.focus: Took Jerusalem in 614, campaigned in Egypt and Anatolia and camped at Chalcedon in 626.
keyPeople.outcome: Negotiated with Heraclius, seized the Persian throne in 630 and was murdered after about forty days.

keyPeople.name: Zacharias of Jerusalem
keyPeople.focus: Captured in 614 and deported to Persia with the True Cross.
keyPeople.outcome: Remained in captivity until the end of the war.

keyPeople.name: Modestus of Jerusalem
keyPeople.role: Abbot, then locum and patriarch of Jerusalem
keyPeople.focus: Led the rebuilding of the Holy Sepulchre and Jerusalem's churches after 614.
keyPeople.outcome: Remembered in the Orthodox Church as a saint and restorer of the holy places.

keyPeople.name: Maximus the Confessor
keyPeople.focus: Lived through the Persian invasion as a refugee and later witnessed Heraclius' forced baptisms in Africa.
keyPeople.outcome: Opposed the emperor's Monothelite policy; mutilated and exiled, he died in 662.

casualties.note: No reliable overall estimate exists for a war of twenty-six years fought across the Near East. Strategius' account gives tens of thousands of Christian dead at Jerusalem in 614, a figure modern historians regard as inflated, though mass graves found at Mamilla and elsewhere confirm large-scale killing. Losses from famine, plague, deportation and the Avar and Turkic raids cannot be quantified.

effects: Byzantium recovered its eastern provinces and the Cross, but both empires were financially, militarily and demographically exhausted.
The Sasanian state collapsed into civil war after 628, opening the way for its conquest by the Arabs in the 630s–650s.
The Arab Muslim conquest of Syria, Palestine and Egypt followed within a decade of Heraclius' triumph.
Jewish communities in Palestine suffered reprisals and Heraclius decreed forced baptism in 632.
Heraclius' reign marks the transition from the late Roman to the medieval Byzantine state, with Greek replacing Latin in government.
effectsOnChurch: The cult of the True Cross was strengthened; the West later linked the feast of the Exaltation (14 September) to Heraclius' restoration.
The Virgin was celebrated as protector of Constantinople, and the Akathist hymn became tied to the deliverance of 626.
Heraclius' attempt to win back Miaphysites through Monoenergism and Monothelitism produced the controversy settled at the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681).
The war's devastation weakened Chalcedonian Christianity in Syria and Egypt just before the Arab conquests.
conflicts.legacy: Medieval Western writers made Heraclius a model crusader: his recovery of the Cross was read in sermons and appeared in the Golden Legend, and some crusade preachers invoked him. Modern historians debate whether the war deserves the title of the first holy war of Christendom. Its greater legacy is ironic: the triumph of 628–630 left Rome and Persia too exhausted to resist the new power that emerged from Arabia.

dissenters.name: Maximus the Confessor
dissenters.text: In a letter from Africa, Maximus expressed dismay at the forced baptism of Jews ordered by Heraclius in 632, fearing that compelled baptism defiled the sacrament and would produce false conversions.

dissenters.name: Christians of the Church of the East
dissenters.text: Many Christians within the Persian empire served Khosrow loyally and did not regard the war as a struggle between Christ and Zoroaster, a reminder that the Christian world was itself divided by the conflict.

theatres.name: Jerusalem, sack and capture of the Cross
Ganzak and the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp (Takht-i Suleiman)

campaigns.title: The Persian conquest of the Roman East, 613–619
campaigns.people: Persian armies under Shahrbaraz and Shahin
campaigns.text: After defeating Heraclius near Antioch the Persians took Damascus, moved down the coast, captured Jerusalem in May 614 and carried the Cross east, then invaded Egypt and took Alexandria.

campaigns.title: Heraclius' march into Mesopotamia, 627–628
campaigns.people: Heraclius with Roman troops and Turkic allies
campaigns.text: From the Black Sea and the Caucasus Heraclius joined the Turks before Tiflis, marched south through the Zagros, destroyed the Persian field army near Nineveh, sacked Dastagird and approached Ctesiphon, triggering Khosrow's overthrow.

campaigns.title: The return of the True Cross, 630
campaigns.text: After receiving the relic from the Persians, Heraclius travelled through Syria and Galilee and entered Jerusalem in procession to restore the Cross to the Holy Sepulchre.

conflicts.name: Charlemagne's Saxon Wars and forced baptism
conflicts.region: Saxony (north-west Germany between the Rhine and the Elbe)
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Conquest and conversion were inseparable. Frankish annals present the wars as a struggle against 'faithless' pagans who broke oaths and relapsed, and the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae prescribed death for refusing baptism or practising pagan rites. Yet the Franks had fought the Saxons over raids and the frontier for generations, and Charlemagne's aims included tribute, security and the incorporation of a large territory into his kingdom. Historians such as Roger Collins and Rosamond McKitterick stress the political and military logic; Richard Fletcher and others emphasise that baptism was treated as the sign of submission, so that Saxon resistance to Franks and to Christianity became the same thing. 'Major' rather than 'central' reflects that blend.

sides.name: Frankish kingdom of Charlemagne
leaders: Pippin and Charles the Younger (his sons)

sides.name: Saxon peoples (Westphalians, Engrians, Eastphalians, Nordalbingians)
sides.faith: Germanic traditional religion (cult of the Irminsul and sacred groves)

conflicts.summary: For more than thirty years Charlemagne fought the pagan Saxons, destroying their sacred pillar the Irminsul in 772, imposing mass baptism, executing thousands of captives at Verden in 782 and deporting whole communities. A capitulary made refusal of baptism a capital crime. Alcuin of York protested that faith cannot be compelled. Saxony was incorporated into the Frankish realm and its church, but at heavy human cost.
conflicts.story:
The Saxons were a confederation of peoples without a king, living between the Frankish Rhineland and the Elbe, who had long raided Frankish lands and resisted Anglo-Saxon missionaries. In 772, at an assembly at Worms, the young Charlemagne decided on a campaign. He took the fortress of Eresburg and destroyed the Irminsul, a great sacred pillar or tree, carrying off the treasure stored at the sanctuary. The Royal Frankish Annals present this as a war against a perfidious people bound to idols.

The pattern of the following years was conquest, oath-taking and baptism, then revolt and renewed punitive campaigns. At an assembly at Paderborn in 777 many Saxons were baptised and swore that if they broke faith they would forfeit their liberty and their land. While Charlemagne was in Spain in 778 Saxon forces under the Westphalian noble Widukind rose and raided as far as the Rhine, burning churches. Missionary bishops and abbots, including Sturm of Fulda and the Northumbrian Willehad, worked in the wake of the armies, and the country was divided into mission districts.

In 782 a Frankish force was annihilated in the Süntel hills. Charlemagne returned and, according to the Royal Frankish Annals, had 4,500 Saxons who had taken part in the revolt beheaded in a single day at Verden on the Aller. Some scholars have suggested a copyist's error (decollare, 'behead', for delocare, 'relocate') or exaggeration, but most accept that a mass execution took place. In the same period Charlemagne issued the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae (dated variously 782 or 785), which decreed death for anyone who refused baptism, burned the dead in the pagan manner, ate meat in Lent out of contempt for Christianity, or attacked a church, and made the payment of tithes compulsory.

Further campaigns in 783–785, including battles at Detmold and on the Hase, broke the revolt. In 785 Widukind submitted and was baptised at Attigny with Charlemagne as his godfather; he disappears from the record thereafter and was later venerated in Saxon tradition. Pope Hadrian I ordered thanksgiving litanies throughout Christendom. Bishoprics were established or planned at Bremen, Paderborn, Minden, Verden, Osnabrück and Münster.

Resistance returned in 792–793, partly provoked by the tithe and the levying of Saxons for Charlemagne's Avar war. Campaigns from 794 to 799 were followed by mass deportations: the annals record thousands of Saxon families, sometimes a third of the population of a district, removed into Frankish territory and replaced by Franks. In 796 Alcuin of York wrote to Charlemagne and his officials urging that preaching precede baptism, that faith be freely given and that tithes not be imposed on new believers. The Capitulare Saxonicum of 797 replaced many capital punishments with fines.

The last campaigns came in 804, when the Saxons north of the Elbe (Nordalbingia) were deported and their land was given to the Slavic Obodrites, Charlemagne's allies. Saxony was integrated into the Carolingian empire. Within a generation it had a Christian aristocracy and monasteries such as Corvey, and the Old Saxon epic Heliand retold the Gospel in the idiom of a Germanic warrior society. In the tenth century a Saxon dynasty, the Ottonians, ruled the East Frankish kingdom and themselves pursued conversion by conquest among the Slavs.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Frankish sources describe the Saxons as 'pagans' and 'oath-breakers' whom God handed over to the Christian king; armies carried relics and were accompanied by clergy, and victories were followed by mass baptisms and papally ordered litanies of thanksgiving. Baptism functioned as the act of political submission, and the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae made rejection of baptism or relapse into paganism punishable by death. Charlemagne was hailed as a new David and a new Constantine bringing a people into the church.
religiousCauses: Carolingian kingship understood the king as defender and spreader of the faith, responsible for bringing pagans into the church.
Baptism and church organisation were seen as the means of making conquest permanent and Saxons into reliable subjects.
The destruction of pagan sanctuaries such as the Irminsul was a deliberate religious and political act.
The memory of Anglo-Saxon missions to the continental Saxons, kin of the English, encouraged the idea of their conversion.
otherCauses: Generations of border raiding between Saxons and Franks along the Rhine and Hessian frontier.
Charlemagne's wider programme of expansion, alongside the conquest of Lombard Italy, Bavaria and the Avar realm.
Plunder, tribute and land for Frankish nobles and churches.
The Saxons' lack of a single king made lasting treaties difficult, encouraging a strategy of total conquest.
triggers: The assembly at Worms in 772 resolved on a campaign, opening with the capture of Eresburg and the destruction of the Irminsul.
Widukind's rising of 778 and the destruction of a Frankish army at the Süntel in 782 provoked Charlemagne's harshest measures.
The revolts of 792–793 against tithes and military levies led to the deportation campaigns.

timeline.text: Charlemagne takes Eresburg and destroys the Irminsul.
Campaign captures the Saxon fortress at Sigiburg (Syburg).
Assembly at Paderborn; mass baptisms and oaths of loyalty.
Widukind's revolt while Charlemagne is in Spain; churches burned.
Frankish defeat at the Süntel; mass execution of Saxons at Verden.
Widukind baptised at Attigny with Charlemagne as godfather; Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae (782 or 785).
Willehad consecrated bishop of Bremen.
New Saxon revolts against tithes and military levies.
Alcuin writes urging persuasion rather than forced baptism and tithes.
Capitulare Saxonicum moderates penalties.
Pope Leo III meets Charlemagne at Paderborn.
Final deportations from Nordalbingia; end of the wars.

keyPeople.name: Charlemagne
keyPeople.role: King of the Franks, emperor from 800
keyPeople.focus: Led or directed almost annual campaigns into Saxony, ordered the Verden executions and issued the Capitulatio.
keyPeople.outcome: Incorporated Saxony into his empire; remembered both as 'father of Europe' and as a converter by the sword.

keyPeople.name: Widukind
keyPeople.focus: Led the risings of 778–785 and found refuge with the Danes.
keyPeople.outcome: Submitted and was baptised in 785; later honoured in Saxon and German tradition, sometimes as a saint and sometimes as a national hero.

keyPeople.name: Alcuin of York
keyPeople.role: Scholar and adviser at Charlemagne's court, abbot of Tours
keyPeople.focus: Criticised forced baptism and the tithe imposed on the Saxons.
keyPeople.outcome: His letters became a classic statement that faith must be freely given.

keyPeople.name: Willehad
keyPeople.focus: Preached among the Saxons and Frisians and fled during Widukind's revolt.
keyPeople.outcome: Consecrated bishop of Bremen in 787; venerated as a saint.

keyPeople.name: Liudger
keyPeople.role: Missionary and first bishop of Münster
keyPeople.focus: Led the mission to western Saxony after the conquest.
keyPeople.outcome: Founded the monastery that gave Münster its name and the abbey of Werden; venerated as a saint.

keyPeople.name: Sturm of Fulda
keyPeople.role: Abbot of Fulda, disciple of Boniface
keyPeople.focus: Accompanied the early campaigns as a missionary and held Eresburg in 779.
keyPeople.outcome: Died shortly after the 779 campaign; venerated as a saint.

casualties.note: There is no basis for an overall estimate. The Royal Frankish Annals give 4,500 Saxons executed at Verden in 782; most historians accept a mass execution of that order, though some question the figure. The annals also record deportations of thousands of families (for example in 795, 798 and 804) but give few numbers that can be relied on.

effects: Saxony was annexed to the Frankish kingdom and later became the heartland of the East Frankish and German kingdom.
Many Saxons were killed, enslaved or deported, and Frankish settlers and Slavic allies were planted on their land.
A network of bishoprics and monasteries (Bremen, Paderborn, Münster, Osnabrück, Minden, Verden, Corvey) was established.
The Frankish frontier reached the Elbe, bringing the Franks into contact with Danes and Slavs.
effectsOnChurch: Conversion was achieved through coercion, mass baptism and compulsory tithes, setting a pattern for later missions by conquest in northern and eastern Europe.
Alcuin's protest articulated the principle that baptism must follow instruction and consent, a principle later cited against forced conversions.
A Saxon Christian culture emerged within a generation, expressed in the Heliand and in Saxon monasteries.
The Ottonian kings, descended from Saxons, later promoted mission and conquest among the Slavs.
conflicts.legacy: The Saxon Wars became a reference point in debates about forced conversion. Medieval chroniclers celebrated Charlemagne as an apostle of the Saxons; in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries German nationalists, and especially National Socialist propagandists, presented Widukind as a Germanic hero murdered by the church, a myth historians reject. Modern scholars use the wars to illustrate how conquest and Christianisation merged in early medieval Europe.

dissenters.name: Alcuin of York
dissenters.text: In letters of 796 to Charlemagne, to the treasurer Meginfrid and to Arn of Salzburg, Alcuin argued that 'faith arises from the will, not from compulsion', that people must be taught before they are baptised, and that the tithe had 'subverted the faith of the Saxons'; he urged gentler preaching for the newly conquered Avars.

campaigns.title: The first Saxon campaign, 772
campaigns.text: From the assembly at Worms the army marched into Saxony, took Eresburg, destroyed the Irminsul and took its treasure, then advanced to the Weser, where Saxons gave hostages.

campaigns.title: Repression of Widukind's revolt, 782–785
campaigns.text: After the defeat at the Süntel Charlemagne executed rebels at Verden, won pitched battles at Detmold and on the Hase, wintered in Saxony and campaigned to the Bardengau until Widukind came to Attigny for baptism.

conflicts.name: The Reconquista in Iberia
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The word 'Reconquista' is a modern label, popularised in the nineteenth century, for nearly eight centuries of intermittent warfare in which Christian kingdoms expanded southwards at the expense of al-Andalus. For long periods the struggle was about land, tribute (the parias paid by the taifa kingdoms) and dynastic rivalry, with frequent alliances across religious lines: the Cid served the Muslim ruler of Zaragoza, and Christian kings fought each other as often as they fought Muslims. Religion became increasingly central from the late eleventh century, when popes granted crusading indulgences for Iberian war (explicitly equated with the Jerusalem crusade by Calixtus II in 1123), the military orders were founded, and the Almoravids and Almohads brought a rigorous ideology of jihad from North Africa. Joseph O'Callaghan stresses the crusading character of the central medieval centuries; other historians warn against reading a continuous religious crusade back into the whole period. 'Major' reflects this variation over time.

sides.name: Christian kingdoms of the north: Asturias–León, Castile, Navarre, Aragon–Catalonia and Portugal
leaders: Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile

sides.name: Al-Andalus: the Umayyad emirate and caliphate of Córdoba and the taifa kingdoms
sides.faith: Sunni Islam, with Christian (Mozarab) and Jewish communities

sides.name: North African Berber empires: the Almoravids and Almohads
sides.faith: Sunni Islam (Almoravid Maliki reformism; Almohad doctrine of divine unity)

sides.name: The Nasrid emirate of Granada and the Marinids
Foreign crusaders and the military orders
leaders: Orders of Calatrava, Santiago and Alcántara

conflicts.summary: After the Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic kingdom in 711, small Christian realms in the northern mountains gradually expanded southwards over almost eight centuries. Periods of coexistence and trade alternated with raids, conquests and religiously charged war. From the late eleventh century the papacy treated Iberian warfare as crusade, and Muslim dynasties from Morocco answered with jihad. The decisive battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) opened the south; Granada, the last Muslim state, surrendered on 2 January 1492, followed within weeks by the expulsion of Spain's Jews and within a decade by the forced conversion of its Muslims.
conflicts.story:
In 711 an Arab and Berber army crossed from North Africa, defeated the Visigothic king Roderic and within a few years controlled most of the peninsula. Tradition dates the beginning of Christian resistance to the victory of Pelagius (Pelayo) at Covadonga in the Asturian mountains, around 718 or 722; the earliest accounts, from the late ninth century, already describe it as a miracle of the Virgin. The small kingdom of Asturias, later León, claimed to be the heir of Visigothic Christian Spain, and its chroniclers spoke of restoring the lost kingdom. The supposed discovery of the tomb of the apostle James at Compostela in the ninth century gave the north a powerful shrine, and the legend of Santiago appearing on a white horse at Clavijo made him 'Matamoros', the Moor-slayer.

For three centuries al-Andalus was the stronger power. Under the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (from 929) it was one of the richest states in Europe, and Christians and Jews lived under it as protected but subordinate dhimmis; some Christians in Córdoba sought martyrdom in the 850s. The regent al-Mansur (Almanzor) led some fifty raids into the Christian north, sacking Barcelona in 985 and Santiago de Compostela in 997 and carrying off captives. After the caliphate collapsed in 1031 into rival taifa kingdoms, the Christian rulers extracted tribute (parias) and began to take territory. Alfonso VI of León–Castile captured Toledo, the old Visigothic capital, in 1085.

The fall of Toledo brought the Almoravids, a Berber reform movement from Morocco, into Spain; under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they defeated Alfonso at Sagrajas (al-Zallaqa) in 1086 and absorbed the taifas. Meanwhile the papacy increasingly sponsored Iberian war: an expedition to Barbastro in 1064, which ended in a massacre and enslavement, attracted French knights; Urban II urged Catalans to restore Tarragona rather than go east; and in 1123 the First Lateran Council and Calixtus II granted the same remission of sins to those fighting in Spain as to those going to Jerusalem. Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, took Valencia in 1094, having previously served the Muslim ruler of Zaragoza. Alfonso I of Aragon took Zaragoza in 1118, and in 1147 Afonso Henriques of Portugal, helped by English, Flemish and German crusaders sailing to the Second Crusade, captured Lisbon after a four-month siege, followed by a sack in which the Mozarab bishop of the city was killed.

The Almohads, a more rigorous movement which ended the toleration of Christians and Jews in their lands (the young Maimonides' family left Córdoba), crossed into Spain in the 1140s–1170s and crushed Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos in 1195. Military orders on the model of the Templars were founded to hold the frontier: Calatrava (1158), Santiago (1170), Alcántara and Avis. Pope Innocent III proclaimed a crusade, and on 16 July 1212 the combined armies of Castile, Aragon and Navarre, with some foreign crusaders, routed the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa. The great conquests followed: James I of Aragon took Majorca (1229) and Valencia (1238), and Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba (1236), Jaén (1246) and Seville (1248), where most of the Muslim population left or was expelled. Mudéjares, Muslims living under Christian rule, remained in large numbers in Valencia and Aragon.

Only the Nasrid emirate of Granada survived, often as a tributary of Castile, for two and a half centuries. The Marinids of Morocco intervened until their defeat with the Granadans at the Río Salado in 1340. Under Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, whose marriage united the two crowns, the Granada War began in 1482 after a Nasrid raid on Zahara. Exploiting a civil war between the emir Abu al-Hasan and his son Muhammad XII (Boabdil), Castilian armies with artillery took town after town; when Málaga resisted in 1487 almost its entire surviving population was enslaved. Papal crusading bulls and the cruzada tax funded the war. Granada surrendered by treaty, and on 2 January 1492 the monarchs entered the Alhambra.

The capitulation guaranteed Muslims their religion, law and property. These promises were soon broken. The Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492 ordered the Jews of Spain to convert or leave; tens of thousands went into exile. Archbishop Hernando de Talavera of Granada favoured slow persuasion, but Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros imposed mass baptisms from 1499, provoking the Alpujarras revolt (1499–1501), after which Muslims of Castile were ordered to convert or leave in 1502, and those of Aragon in 1526. The converted Moriscos remained suspect, rose again in 1568–1571, and were expelled in 1609–1614. In 1492 also, Columbus sailed under the patronage of the same monarchs, and many habits of the Iberian frontier passed to the conquest of the Americas.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Christian kings presented themselves as restorers of a Christian Spain lost through sin, and from the ninth century invoked Saint James 'Matamoros' as the heavenly warrior of the army; 'Santiago!' became the Castilian battle cry. From the 1060s popes offered remission of sins for Iberian campaigns, Calixtus II equated them with the Jerusalem crusade in 1123, and Innocent III proclaimed the crusade of 1212. Military orders of knight-brothers took monastic vows to fight the Muslims. Crusade bulls and the papal cruzada tax financed the Granada War, and the cross was raised on the Alhambra in 1492. On the Muslim side, the Almoravids and Almohads framed their intervention as jihad to defend Islam and purify al-Andalus, and al-Mansur's raids were celebrated as holy war.
religiousCauses: A northern Christian ideology, visible from the ninth-century Asturian chronicles, of restoring the Visigothic Christian kingdom lost in 711.
Papal extension of crusading indulgences to Iberia from the late eleventh century and the founding of military orders.
The cult of Saint James at Compostela and the image of Santiago Matamoros as patron of the war.
Almoravid and Almohad ideologies of jihad and religious reform, which hardened the frontier and ended earlier forms of coexistence.
In the fifteenth century, Isabella and Ferdinand's programme of religious unity, linked to the Inquisition (1478) and expulsion of the Jews.
otherCauses: Competition for land, pasture, towns and settlers as the northern kingdoms grew.
Tribute (parias) and plunder from the wealthy taifa kingdoms after 1031.
Rivalries among the Christian kingdoms themselves and among the Muslim taifas, which produced cross-religious alliances.
The political fragmentation of al-Andalus after the fall of the Córdoba caliphate.
The ambition of the noble and military-order elites for lordships and of the crowns for royal power and revenue.
triggers: The Umayyad conquest of 711 and the resistance at Covadonga (c. 718/722).
The collapse of the caliphate of Córdoba in 1031 and Alfonso VI's capture of Toledo in 1085, which drew in the Almoravids.
The disaster at Alarcos in 1195, which led to the crusade of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
The Nasrid capture of Zahara in December 1481, which opened the Granada War.

timeline.text: Umayyad Arab and Berber forces defeat the Visigoths and conquer most of Iberia.
Pelagius' victory at Covadonga (traditionally 718 or 722).
Al-Mansur sacks Santiago de Compostela.
The caliphate of Córdoba collapses into taifa kingdoms.
Expedition to Barbastro, with French participation and papal encouragement.
Alfonso VI captures Toledo.
Almoravids defeat Alfonso VI at Sagrajas (al-Zallaqa).
El Cid takes Valencia.
Calixtus II equates Iberian war with the Jerusalem crusade.
Afonso Henriques and northern crusaders capture Lisbon.
Almohads defeat Castile at Alarcos.
Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa.
Ferdinand III captures Seville after Córdoba (1236).
Granada surrenders on 2 January; Alhambra Decree expels the Jews (31 March).

keyPeople.name: Pelagius (Pelayo)
keyPeople.focus: Led the victory at Covadonga that later tradition made the beginning of the Reconquista.
keyPeople.outcome: Founder of the Asturian monarchy; a figure of legend as much as history.

keyPeople.name: Al-Mansur (Almanzor)
keyPeople.role: Chamberlain and de facto ruler of al-Andalus
keyPeople.focus: Led dozens of raids into the Christian north, sacking Barcelona and Santiago de Compostela.
keyPeople.outcome: Died after a campaign in 1002; his dynasty's fall began the collapse of the caliphate.

keyPeople.name: Alfonso VI of León and Castile
keyPeople.role: King and self-styled 'emperor of all Spain'
keyPeople.focus: Collected tribute from the taifas and captured Toledo in 1085.
keyPeople.outcome: Defeated by the Almoravids at Sagrajas in 1086 and at Uclés in 1108, where his only son died.

keyPeople.name: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid
keyPeople.role: Castilian nobleman and soldier of fortune
keyPeople.focus: Served both Christian and Muslim rulers before conquering and ruling Valencia from 1094.
keyPeople.outcome: Became Spain's national hero through the Cantar de mio Cid; Valencia was abandoned in 1102.

keyPeople.name: Yusuf ibn Tashfin
keyPeople.focus: Crossed to Spain at the taifas' request, won at Sagrajas and annexed al-Andalus.
keyPeople.outcome: Founded Marrakesh and united Morocco and al-Andalus.

keyPeople.name: Alfonso VIII of Castile
keyPeople.focus: Defeated at Alarcos in 1195, he led the victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
keyPeople.outcome: His victory broke Almohad power in Spain.

keyPeople.name: Ferdinand III of Castile
keyPeople.focus: Conquered Córdoba, Jaén and Seville.
keyPeople.outcome: Canonised in 1671; buried in Seville cathedral with epitaphs in Latin, Castilian, Arabic and Hebrew.

keyPeople.name: Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon
keyPeople.focus: Waged the Granada War of 1482–1492 with papal crusade funding.
keyPeople.outcome: Took Granada, expelled the Jews, sponsored Columbus and later required Muslims to convert or leave.

keyPeople.name: Muhammad XII (Boabdil)
keyPeople.focus: Fought his father and uncle for the throne and surrendered Granada by treaty.
keyPeople.outcome: Went into exile in the Alpujarras and then Morocco.

keyPeople.name: Hernando de Talavera
keyPeople.role: Hieronymite friar, Isabella's confessor and first archbishop of Granada
keyPeople.focus: Sought to convert Granada's Muslims by preaching, charity and Arabic catechesis.
keyPeople.outcome: Sidelined by Cisneros' coercive policy; investigated by the Inquisition shortly before his death.

casualties.note: No meaningful estimate exists for nearly eight centuries of intermittent warfare, raiding and enslavement. Chronicle figures for battles such as Sagrajas, Alarcos or Las Navas de Tolosa are greatly exaggerated on both sides. Enslavement was a major form of harm: al-Mansur's raids carried off thousands of Christians, and the population of Málaga, perhaps around 11,000–15,000 people, was enslaved in 1487, though even this figure is approximate. The Jewish exiles of 1492 are variously estimated by historians at roughly 40,000 to over 100,000.

effects: The Muslim political presence in Iberia ended, and Castile, Aragon and Portugal became dominant Christian monarchies.
Large Muslim populations were displaced, enslaved or reduced to subject Mudéjar status, and later forcibly converted (1499–1526) and expelled as Moriscos (1609–1614).
The Jews of Spain were expelled in 1492 and those of Portugal forced to convert in 1497.
A militarised frontier society, with military orders, municipal militias and the ideal of the warrior-settler, shaped Iberian culture and was carried to the Americas.
Toledo and other conquered cities became centres where Arabic science and philosophy were translated into Latin.
effectsOnChurch: The crusading indulgence was extended to Iberia, and military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago became powerful religious corporations.
The cult of Santiago and the pilgrimage to Compostela grew into one of Christendom's major devotions.
Toledo translations, including the Latin Qur'an commissioned by Peter the Venerable (1143), shaped Western Christian knowledge of Islam.
The quest for religious unity under the Catholic Monarchs produced the Spanish Inquisition (1478), concerns about 'purity of blood' and suspicion of converts.
The Mozarabic rite and community largely disappeared as Roman liturgy and northern clergy replaced older Iberian Christian traditions.
conflicts.legacy: The Reconquista became a founding myth of Spanish and Portuguese national identity, emphasised under the Franco regime and still invoked by some modern nationalist movements. Historians now stress that the period also included long stretches of coexistence, cultural exchange and cross-religious alliance (sometimes idealised as convivencia), as well as violence on all sides. The forced conversions and expulsions that followed 1492 are widely recognised as a tragedy for Spain's Jews and Muslims.

dissenters.name: Peter the Venerable
dissenters.text: The abbot of Cluny commissioned a Latin translation of the Qur'an in Spain in 1142–1143 and wrote that he approached Muslims 'not with arms but with words, not with force but with reason, not in hatred but in love', though he did not reject crusading itself.

dissenters.name: Ramon Llull
dissenters.text: The Majorcan lay theologian (c. 1232–1316) devoted his life to learning Arabic and to peaceful disputation with Muslims, urging missions rather than conquest, although in later life he also proposed crusade plans.

dissenters.name: Hernando de Talavera
dissenters.text: As archbishop of Granada after 1492 Talavera insisted on honouring the surrender treaty and converting Muslims by preaching, schooling and Arabic-language instruction, opposing the forced baptisms imposed by Cisneros.

dissenters.name: Juan de Segovia
dissenters.text: The Castilian theologian (c. 1393–1458) argued, after the fall of Constantinople, that Christians should seek conferences and dialogue with Muslims rather than war, and prepared a new trilingual Qur'an translation.

theatres.name: Santiago de Compostela, sacked by al-Mansur
Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
Siege of Málaga and enslavement of its people

campaigns.title: The northern crusaders' voyage to Lisbon, 1147
campaigns.people: English, Flemish, Norman and Rhineland crusaders bound for the Holy Land
campaigns.text: A crusade fleet of some two hundred ships gathered at Dartmouth, was persuaded at Porto by Bishop Peter Pitões and King Afonso Henriques to help besiege Lisbon, and took the city in October 1147 after a four-month siege.

campaigns.title: The Las Navas de Tolosa campaign, 1212
campaigns.people: Alfonso VIII of Castile, Peter II of Aragon, Sancho VII of Navarre and foreign crusaders
campaigns.text: The crusade army assembled at Toledo, retook Calatrava (after which many foreign crusaders went home), crossed the Sierra Morena, routed the Almohads on 16 July and then sacked Baeza and Úbeda.

campaigns.title: The Granada War, 1482–1492
campaigns.people: Ferdinand and Isabella's Castilian and Aragonese armies
campaigns.text: Beginning with the seizure of Alhama, Castilian armies with artillery reduced the Nasrid emirate piece by piece, besieging Málaga and Baza, and from the camp-city of Santa Fe forced Granada's surrender.

conflicts.name: The First Crusade and the Rhineland massacres
conflicts.region: Western Europe, the Rhineland, the Balkans, Anatolia, Syria and Palestine
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Religion was the main stated and, most historians now agree, the main real motive. Urban II offered remission of the penance due for sin to those who went to free the Eastern churches and Jerusalem 'for devotion alone, not to gain honour or money'. Older interpretations stressed land-hungry younger sons and economic pressures; Jonathan Riley-Smith and others showed from charters that crusaders sold or mortgaged property at great cost and were often eldest sons and established lords, motivated by penitential piety, pilgrimage and the reform movement. Other factors still mattered: the Byzantine appeal for help, papal ambitions after the schism of 1054 and the Investiture Controversy, the ambitions of princes such as Bohemond and Baldwin, and the lure of booty once on campaign. On the Muslim side the Seljuk and Fatimid rulers were initially slow to treat the invasion as a religious war.

sides.name: Latin crusaders ('Franks')
leaders: Raymond of Saint-Gilles, count of Toulouse

sides.name: Seljuk Turks and Syrian Muslim rulers
Jewish communities of the Rhineland (victims)
leaders: Communal leaders of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, such as Kalonymus ben Meshullam of Mainz

conflicts.summary: Responding to a Byzantine appeal for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II at Clermont in November 1095 called on Western knights to liberate the Eastern Christians and Jerusalem in return for remission of sins. Tens of thousands took the cross. Popular bands massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096; the main armies took Nicaea, survived the terrible siege of Antioch and captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing much of its Muslim and Jewish population. The crusade created the Latin states of the East and the enduring institution of crusading.
conflicts.story:
In the eleventh century the Seljuk Turks had taken most of Anatolia from the Byzantine Empire after the battle of Manzikert (1071) and had seized Jerusalem from the Fatimids in 1073 (the Fatimids retook it in 1098). Western pilgrims reported difficulties on the road to the Holy Sepulchre, which had been destroyed by the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim in 1009 and later rebuilt. In March 1095 envoys of the emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza for military help. Urban, a reforming pope who had been driven from Rome during the Investiture Controversy, saw an opportunity to direct the violence of the knightly class towards a holy purpose, to aid the Eastern Church after the breach of 1054 and to assert papal leadership.

On 27 November 1095, at the end of the Council of Clermont, Urban preached in a field outside the town. No verbatim text survives; later accounts by Fulcher of Chartres, Robert the Monk and others differ, but agree that he described the sufferings of Eastern Christians and the pollution of the holy places, and offered that the journey would count for all penance. The crowd is said to have cried 'Deus vult!' (God wills it), and many sewed cloth crosses onto their garments. Urban toured France preaching, and popular preachers such as Peter the Hermit spread the message more widely than the pope intended.

In spring 1096 popular bands set out before the princes. Some, led by Count Emicho of Flonheim and others, turned on the Jewish communities of the Rhineland, arguing that it was wrong to march against God's enemies far away while leaving 'the killers of Christ' at home, and seeking money. At Speyer in early May the bishop protected most of the Jews; at Worms in mid-May some 800 were killed, including those sheltering in the bishop's palace; at Mainz on 27 May the archbishop's protection collapsed and the community was destroyed, many choosing to kill their families and themselves rather than be baptised. Killings and forced baptisms followed at Cologne, Trier, Metz, Regensburg and Prague. Hebrew chronicles such as that of Solomon bar Samson remember these as the martyrdoms of 1096. Peter the Hermit's army reached Constantinople and crossed into Asia, where the Turks destroyed it at Civetot in October 1096; Emicho's band was dispersed in Hungary.

The princely armies converged on Constantinople over the winter of 1096–1097, where most leaders swore to return former imperial lands to Alexios. Together with Byzantine forces they besieged Nicaea, which surrendered to the Byzantines on 19 June 1097, and defeated Kilij Arslan at Dorylaeum on 1 July. After a gruelling march across Anatolia, Baldwin of Boulogne broke away to take Edessa, founding the first crusader state in 1098. The main army besieged Antioch from October 1097; starvation and desertion were severe. On 3 June 1098 Bohemond secured the city through a traitor in a tower, and the crusaders massacred much of the population. Days later they were themselves besieged by the relief army of Kerbogha of Mosul. The 'discovery' of the Holy Lance by the visionary Peter Bartholomew revived morale, and on 28 June the crusaders defeated Kerbogha outside the walls. Adhemar of Le Puy died in August, and quarrels between Bohemond and Raymond delayed the march. At Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in December 1098 the crusaders massacred the inhabitants, and chroniclers including Radulph of Caen and Albert of Aachen record that starving soldiers ate the flesh of the dead.

The army, perhaps reduced to some 12,000–15,000 fighting men, reached Jerusalem, now held by the Fatimids, on 7 June 1099. After a failed assault, a barefoot penitential procession round the walls and the arrival of Genoese timber for siege towers, Godfrey of Bouillon's men broke in on 15 July. The crusaders killed large numbers of the Muslim inhabitants, including people who had taken refuge on the Temple Mount (the Haram al-Sharif), and burned the city's main synagogue with Jews inside, according to Muslim sources; others were ransomed, as letters in the Cairo Geniza show. Latin writers boasted that men waded in blood; Muslim writers later gave figures of 70,000 or more, which modern historians such as Benjamin Kedar regard as greatly inflated, with a toll of perhaps around 3,000 suggested by the near-contemporary Ibn al-Arabi. Godfrey became ruler with the title 'advocate of the Holy Sepulchre'.

On 12 August 1099 the crusaders defeated a Fatimid relief army at Ascalon, and most survivors went home. Four Latin states, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch, the Kingdom of Jerusalem and later the County of Tripoli, were established. The success was taken in the West as a miracle confirming that God willed the crusade; it inspired further expeditions and the creation of the military orders, but it also embittered relations with Byzantium, which had expected the return of Antioch, and in time provoked a Muslim counter-crusade.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Urban II framed the expedition as an armed pilgrimage and act of penance: those who went for devotion alone would have the journey counted in place of all penance for confessed sins. Participants took vows and wore the cross, recalling Christ's command to 'take up his cross' (Matthew 16:24), and the cry 'Deus vult!' became the crusaders' slogan. Clergy accompanied the armies, fasts, processions and visions (the Holy Lance at Antioch, appearances of warrior saints such as St George) punctuated the campaign, and the dead were spoken of as martyrs. The Rhineland attackers justified killing Jews as vengeance for the crucifixion, contrary to the teaching of popes and bishops that Jews should not be harmed.
religiousCauses: The papacy's call to liberate Eastern Christians and the Holy Sepulchre, and its offer of remission of penance to participants.
A penitential piety among the knightly class, shaped by the Gregorian reform, the Peace and Truce of God and the tradition of pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
Reports of the sufferings of Eastern Christians and pilgrims, and memory of al-Hakim's destruction of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009.
Apocalyptic expectations attached to Jerusalem among popular preachers and crusaders.
Anti-Jewish ideas of collective guilt for the crucifixion, which fuelled the Rhineland massacres.
otherCauses: Alexios I's need for Western mercenaries to recover Anatolia after Manzikert (1071).
Papal ambitions to lead Christendom during the Investiture Controversy and to heal the breach of 1054 with the Eastern Church.
The ambitions of individual princes, such as Bohemond and Baldwin, for lordships in the East.
Divisions among the Seljuk rulers after the death of Sultan Malik-Shah in 1092 and the Seljuk–Fatimid rivalry, which made the Muslim Near East vulnerable.
Booty and the prospect of material reward once the campaign was underway.
triggers: The appeal of Alexios I's envoys at the Council of Piacenza in March 1095.
Urban II's sermon at Clermont on 27 November 1095.
The preaching of Peter the Hermit and others, which launched the popular crusades and the attacks on Jews in spring 1096.

timeline.text: Seljuk victory at Manzikert opens Anatolia to the Turks.
Byzantine envoys at Piacenza (March); Urban II preaches the crusade at Clermont (27 November).
Rhineland massacres of Jews at Speyer, Worms, Mainz and elsewhere (May–June); People's Crusade destroyed at Civetot (October).
Princes' armies at Constantinople; Nicaea surrenders (19 June); victory at Dorylaeum (1 July); siege of Antioch begins (October).
Baldwin takes Edessa; Antioch falls (3 June); Kerbogha defeated (28 June); massacre at Ma'arrat al-Nu'man (December).
Siege of Jerusalem from 7 June; city stormed and massacre (15 July); victory at Ascalon (12 August).
Death of Godfrey; Baldwin I becomes first king of Jerusalem.

keyPeople.name: Urban II
keyPeople.focus: Proclaimed the crusade at Clermont and organised its preaching and leadership.
keyPeople.outcome: Died on 29 July 1099, two weeks after Jerusalem fell, before the news reached him; beatified in 1881.

keyPeople.name: Peter the Hermit
keyPeople.focus: Raised and led the largest of the popular armies, destroyed at Civetot; later joined the main army.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned to Europe and founded a priory at Neufmoustier near Huy.

keyPeople.name: Emicho of Flonheim
keyPeople.role: Leader of a popular crusade band
keyPeople.focus: Led the massacres of Jews at Mainz and elsewhere in May 1096.
keyPeople.outcome: His army was defeated in Hungary; condemned by contemporary Christian and Jewish chroniclers.

keyPeople.name: Adhemar of Le Puy
keyPeople.role: Bishop of Le Puy and papal legate
keyPeople.focus: Spiritual leader of the crusade, conciliating the princes and the Byzantines.
keyPeople.outcome: Died of disease at Antioch on 1 August 1098.

keyPeople.name: Godfrey of Bouillon
keyPeople.focus: Led one of the main armies and was among the first to enter Jerusalem.
keyPeople.outcome: Ruled Jerusalem as 'advocate of the Holy Sepulchre' until his death in 1100; idealised in later legend.

keyPeople.name: Raymond of Saint-Gilles
keyPeople.focus: Led the largest army, sponsored the Holy Lance and besieged Jerusalem from the south.
keyPeople.outcome: Began the conquest of the County of Tripoli and died besieging it.

keyPeople.name: Bohemond of Taranto
keyPeople.focus: Secured the capture of Antioch and kept it for himself despite oaths to Alexios.
keyPeople.outcome: Prince of Antioch; later led an unsuccessful war against Byzantium in 1107–1108.

keyPeople.name: Alexios I Komnenos
keyPeople.focus: Appealed for Western help, secured the princes' oaths and recovered Nicaea and western Anatolia.
keyPeople.outcome: Regained much of Anatolia but distrusted the Latins after Antioch; portrayed in his daughter Anna Komnene's Alexiad.

keyPeople.name: Kilij Arslan I
keyPeople.focus: Destroyed the People's Crusade but lost Nicaea and the battle of Dorylaeum.
keyPeople.outcome: Moved his capital to Konya and continued to fight later crusades.

keyPeople.name: Iftikhar al-Dawla
keyPeople.focus: Expelled the city's Christians and defended Jerusalem in 1099.
keyPeople.outcome: Surrendered the Tower of David to Raymond and was allowed to leave for Ascalon with his garrison.

casualties.note: No reliable overall figure exists. Modern estimates of those who set out range widely, perhaps 60,000–100,000 including non-combatants, and many more died of hunger and disease than in battle. The Rhineland massacres killed probably several thousand Jews; Hebrew sources name about 800 dead at Worms and over 1,000 at Mainz. For Jerusalem in 1099 Muslim figures of 70,000 or more are rejected by modern historians; Benjamin Kedar notes a near-contemporary estimate of about 3,000, while others think the toll was higher. Losses at Antioch and Ma'arra were also heavy but cannot be counted.

effects: Four Latin states were established in Syria and Palestine, lasting in some form until 1291.
Jewish communities of the Rhineland were devastated, beginning a long pattern of crusade-related violence against European Jews.
Relations between Latin Christians and Byzantium were strained by disputes over Antioch and mutual distrust.
Muslim rulers gradually developed a counter-crusade ideology of jihad, culminating under Zengi, Nur ad-Din and Saladin.
Italian maritime cities (Genoa, Pisa, Venice) gained trading privileges in the eastern Mediterranean.
effectsOnChurch: Crusading became an enduring institution of the Latin Church, with vows, indulgences and papal direction, later applied to Spain, the Baltic and heretics.
Military religious orders (the Templars and Hospitallers) emerged in the crusader states.
Latin patriarchs were installed in Antioch and Jerusalem, displacing Greek hierarchs and deepening the East–West schism.
The papacy's prestige and claim to lead Christendom were greatly enhanced.
Eastern Christians under crusader rule (Syriac, Armenian, Greek) experienced both protection and subordination to Latin clergy.
conflicts.legacy: The First Crusade was remembered in the West as a miraculous triumph and became the model for later crusades and crusading rhetoric. In Jewish memory it is the trauma of 1096, commemorated in liturgical laments. In the Muslim world it was at first a marginal event and only later became a symbol of Western aggression, a theme revived in modern politics. Popes have since expressed regret for violence committed in the name of the faith, notably John Paul II during the Day of Pardon in 2000.

dissenters.name: Bishop John of Speyer and other Rhineland bishops
dissenters.text: In May 1096 Bishop John of Speyer protected the Jews of his city and punished attackers, and Archbishop Hermann III of Cologne hid Jews in surrounding villages, acting on the long-standing church teaching that Jews were not to be killed or forcibly baptised; the archbishop of Mainz tried but failed to protect his city's Jews.

dissenters.name: Anselm of Canterbury
dissenters.text: Anselm wrote to monks forbidding them to leave their cloisters to join the expedition, insisting that their true Jerusalem was the 'vision of peace' within the monastery.

dissenters.name: Anna Komnene
dissenters.text: The Byzantine princess and historian expressed in the Alexiad her disapproval of Latin priests who took up arms and fought, contrasting this with Orthodox canon law forbidding clergy to shed blood, and her mistrust of the crusaders' motives.

theatres.name: Massacre of the Jews of Worms
Massacre of the Jews of Mainz
Civetot, destruction of the People's Crusade

campaigns.title: The princes' route to Jerusalem, 1096–1099
campaigns.people: The main crusade armies of Godfrey, Raymond, Bohemond, the two Roberts and others
campaigns.text: The armies travelled by separate routes to Constantinople, then together took Nicaea, fought at Dorylaeum, crossed Anatolia via Heraclea and Marash, besieged Antioch for eight months, marched south past Ma'arra and down the Lebanese coast to Jerusalem.

campaigns.title: Peter the Hermit's People's Crusade, 1096
campaigns.people: Peter the Hermit, Walter Sans-Avoir and popular crusaders
campaigns.text: Peter's followers marched from Cologne through Hungary, fought the Byzantines at Niš, were ferried across the Bosporus by Alexios and were annihilated by the Turks near Civetot in October 1096.

campaigns.title: Emicho's band and the Rhineland massacres, 1096
campaigns.people: Count Emicho of Flonheim and allied bands
campaigns.text: Moving up the Rhine in May 1096, bands associated with Emicho attacked Jewish communities at Speyer, Worms and Mainz before being routed by the Hungarians at Moson.

conflicts.name: The Second and Third Crusades
conflicts.region: Western Europe, Anatolia, Syria, Palestine and Cyprus
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Both crusades were proclaimed by popes in direct response to Muslim victories (the fall of Edessa in 1144 and the loss of Jerusalem in 1187), were preached as penitential pilgrimages with indulgences, and drew kings into armed pilgrimage on an unprecedented scale. Political rivalries nonetheless shaped them deeply: the choice to attack Damascus in 1148, the Anglo-French quarrels of 1190–1192 and the succession disputes in the Kingdom of Jerusalem. On the Muslim side Zengi, Nur ad-Din and Saladin deliberately cultivated the ideology of jihad to unite Syria and Egypt, though historians such as Lyons and Jackson stress how much Saladin's career also served dynastic ambition.

sides.name: Latin crusaders and the crusader states
Zengid and Ayyubid Syria and Egypt
Jewish communities of the Rhineland and England (victims)

conflicts.summary: The fall of Edessa to Zengi in 1144 prompted Eugenius III and Bernard of Clairvaux to launch the Second Crusade (1145–1149), led by the kings of France and Germany; it ended in defeat in Anatolia and a failed four-day siege of Damascus. Four decades later Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin and took Jerusalem (1187). The Third Crusade (1189–1192) under Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II and Richard I recaptured Acre and the coast but not Jerusalem, ending in a negotiated truce that allowed Christian pilgrims access to the holy places.
conflicts.story:
On 24 December 1144 Imad al-Din Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, captured Edessa, capital of the first crusader state. Pope Eugenius III, a Cistercian, issued the bull Quantum praedecessores on 1 December 1145, the first crusade bull to set out formally the privileges of crusaders. Bernard of Clairvaux, the most influential churchman of the age, preached at Vézelay on 31 March 1146 before Louis VII of France and later persuaded the reluctant Conrad III of Germany to take the cross at Speyer at Christmas 1146. Bernard's preaching letters promised a 'year of jubilee' and remission of sins. The crusade was extended to Iberia, where it helped the capture of Lisbon in 1147, and to the pagan Wends east of the Elbe.

As in 1096, popular preaching turned against Jews. A Cistercian monk named Radulf preached in the Rhineland that Jews should be killed, and attacks followed at Cologne, Mainz, Würzburg and elsewhere. Bernard travelled to the Rhineland, silenced Radulf and wrote that the Jews were not to be persecuted, killed or put to flight, since they were living reminders of Christ's passion and destined for conversion; Jewish chroniclers such as Ephraim of Bonn credited him with saving many lives.

The kings' armies travelled overland through Hungary to Constantinople, where Manuel I Komnenos, then at war with Roger II of Sicily and distrustful after the First Crusade, hurried them across the Bosporus. Conrad's army was routed by the Seljuks near Dorylaeum in October 1147; Louis' army was mauled at Mount Cadmus in January 1148, and many of his poorer followers were abandoned at Attalia. The surviving leaders met at Acre in June 1148 and decided to attack Damascus, a Muslim city that had often been allied with Jerusalem against Zengi. The siege lasted only from 24 to 28 July before the army withdrew amid recriminations. The failure was a shock to the West; Bernard, in his treatise On Consideration, defended the crusade by blaming the sins of the crusaders and comparing the outcome to Israel's failures in the wilderness.

In the following decades Zengi's son Nur ad-Din united Muslim Syria, took Damascus in 1154 and promoted jihad through mosques, madrasas and propaganda centred on Jerusalem. His Kurdish officer Saladin became master of Egypt in 1169, abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and after Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 gradually added Damascus, Aleppo (1183) and Mosul's submission (1186). The Kingdom of Jerusalem, weakened by the leprosy of Baldwin IV and factional disputes, was provoked by Reynald of Châtillon's raids on caravans and on the Red Sea. On 4 July 1187 Saladin destroyed the kingdom's field army at the Horns of Hattin, capturing King Guy of Lusignan and the relic of the True Cross. He personally killed Reynald and had about two hundred captured Templars and Hospitallers executed. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187; Saladin allowed inhabitants to ransom themselves, with no general massacre, although thousands who could not pay were enslaved. Only Tyre, defended by Conrad of Montferrat, and a few castles held out.

Pope Gregory VIII issued the bull Audita tremendi in October 1187, interpreting the disaster as punishment for sin. Henry II of England and Philip II of France imposed the 'Saladin tithe', the first general European tax. Frederick I Barbarossa left Regensburg in May 1189 with a large, disciplined army, forced passage through Byzantine territory and defeated the Seljuks at Iconium (Konya), but drowned in the river Saleph in Cilicia on 10 June 1190, after which most of his army dispersed. In England Richard I's coronation in September 1189 was followed by anti-Jewish riots in London and elsewhere, and in March 1190 the Jews of York, besieged in the royal castle, mostly killed themselves or were murdered after surrender.
