Meanwhile Guy of Lusignan, released by Saladin, began a siege of Acre in August 1189, and was himself besieged by Saladin's army in a war of attrition lasting two years. Philip II arrived in April 1191 and Richard in June, having conquered Cyprus from Isaac Komnenos on the way. Acre surrendered on 12 July 1191. When the ransom terms were delayed Richard had about 2,600–3,000 Muslim prisoners killed in sight of Saladin's camp on 20 August. Philip returned to France. Richard defeated Saladin at Arsuf on 7 September 1191, rebuilt Jaffa and twice advanced within sight of Jerusalem but judged that he could not hold it. After further fighting at Jaffa in 1192, Richard and Saladin agreed the Treaty of Jaffa on 2 September 1192: a three-year truce leaving the coast from Tyre to Jaffa to the Latins and Jerusalem to Saladin, with Christian pilgrims allowed to visit the Holy Sepulchre. Richard was captured on his way home and held for ransom by Duke Leopold of Austria and Emperor Henry VI; Saladin died in Damascus in March 1193.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Eugenius III's Quantum praedecessores and Gregory VIII's Audita tremendi offered remission of sins and placed crusaders' families and property under church protection. Bernard of Clairvaux preached the crusade as God's gift of an opportunity for salvation to sinners, a 'time of acceptance'. Crusaders took vows and the cross, the True Cross was carried into battle at Hattin, and the loss of Jerusalem was interpreted as divine punishment for sin. Richard I invoked the Holy Sepulchre and crusade privileges, and the Saladin tithe was levied as a holy obligation. On the Muslim side Nur ad-Din and Saladin promoted jihad to recover al-Quds (Jerusalem), the third holiest site of Islam, and Saladin's secretaries Imad al-Din and al-Qadi al-Fadil framed his wars as holy war; Saladin restored the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa as Islamic shrines in 1187.
religiousCauses: The fall of Edessa in 1144 and of Jerusalem in 1187 were perceived in the West as catastrophes for Christendom requiring a penitential response.
Papal crusade bulls and the preaching of Bernard of Clairvaux and others offered spiritual rewards for taking the cross.
Devotion to Jerusalem and the Holy Sepulchre and the duty to defend the Christian settlers in the East.
The Muslim jihad revival under Zengi, Nur ad-Din and Saladin, centred on the recovery of Jerusalem.
Anti-Jewish preaching by figures such as Radulf, which turned crusading fervour against European Jews.
otherCauses: The political and military weakness of the crusader states, divided by factions and dependent on Western help.
The unification of Syria and Egypt under Nur ad-Din and Saladin, which shifted the regional balance of power.
Royal ambitions and rivalries, notably between the Capetian and Angevin kings, and the prestige of crusading kingship.
The commercial interests of Italian maritime cities in the Levantine ports.
Byzantine–Latin tensions and Byzantine diplomacy with the Seljuks and Saladin.
triggers: Zengi's capture of Edessa on 24 December 1144.
Reynald of Châtillon's attacks on Muslim caravans in breach of truces, which provoked Saladin's invasion of 1187.
The defeat at Hattin on 4 July 1187 and the surrender of Jerusalem on 2 October 1187.

timeline.text: Zengi captures Edessa (24 December).
Eugenius III issues Quantum praedecessores (1 December).
Bernard preaches at Vézelay (31 March); Radulf's anti-Jewish preaching in the Rhineland; Conrad III takes the cross.
Conrad's army defeated near Dorylaeum; capture of Lisbon; Wendish Crusade.
Louis VII's army mauled at Mount Cadmus; failed siege of Damascus (24–28 July).
Nur ad-Din takes Damascus, uniting Muslim Syria.
Saladin ends the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt.
Battle of Hattin (4 July); Jerusalem surrenders to Saladin (2 October); Audita tremendi.
Frederick Barbarossa departs; siege of Acre begins; anti-Jewish riots at Richard I's coronation.
Massacre and mass suicide of the Jews of York (March); Barbarossa drowns in the Saleph (10 June).
Richard conquers Cyprus; Acre surrenders (12 July); execution of Muslim prisoners (20 August); battle of Arsuf (7 September).
Treaty of Jaffa (2 September) ends the Third Crusade.
Death of Saladin in Damascus.

keyPeople.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
keyPeople.role: Cistercian abbot and chief preacher of the Second Crusade
keyPeople.focus: Preached at Vézelay and across France and Germany, and halted Radulf's anti-Jewish preaching.
keyPeople.outcome: His reputation was damaged by the crusade's failure, which he attributed to the sins of the crusaders; canonised in 1174.

keyPeople.name: Eugenius III
keyPeople.focus: Issued Quantum praedecessores and authorised crusades in the East, Iberia and the Baltic.
keyPeople.outcome: Beatified in 1872.

keyPeople.name: Louis VII of France
keyPeople.focus: Led the French army to the East with Eleanor of Aquitaine and joined the siege of Damascus.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned in 1149; his marriage to Eleanor was annulled in 1152.

keyPeople.name: Conrad III
keyPeople.focus: Led the German army, defeated near Dorylaeum, and took part in the siege of Damascus.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned home in 1149 without having been crowned emperor.

keyPeople.name: Nur ad-Din
keyPeople.focus: Defeated the crusaders of 1148 indirectly by strengthening Syria, united Muslim Syria and promoted jihad.
keyPeople.outcome: Remembered as a model pious Muslim ruler; his death opened the way for Saladin.

keyPeople.name: Saladin (Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub)
keyPeople.role: Sultan of Egypt and Syria, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty
keyPeople.focus: Won at Hattin, retook Jerusalem with a negotiated surrender and defended the Levant against the Third Crusade.
keyPeople.outcome: Admired in both Muslim and Western tradition for his chivalry; his empire divided among his heirs.

keyPeople.name: Frederick I Barbarossa
keyPeople.focus: Led the largest army of the Third Crusade across the Balkans and Anatolia.
keyPeople.outcome: Drowned in the river Saleph on 10 June 1190; later the subject of German legend.

keyPeople.name: Richard I of England
keyPeople.focus: Conquered Cyprus, completed the capture of Acre, executed the Muslim prisoners, won at Arsuf and negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa.
keyPeople.outcome: Captured and ransomed on his return; died in France in 1199; nicknamed 'Lionheart'.

keyPeople.name: Philip II Augustus
keyPeople.focus: Shared in the siege of Acre before returning to France in 1191.
keyPeople.outcome: Used Richard's absence to attack Angevin lands in France.

keyPeople.name: Guy of Lusignan
keyPeople.focus: Lost the army and the True Cross at Hattin; after release began the siege of Acre.
keyPeople.outcome: Lost the crown to Conrad of Montferrat and became lord of Cyprus.

casualties.note: No reliable overall figure exists. Chroniclers' numbers for the armies of 1147–1148 and 1189–1192 are greatly exaggerated; losses from disease and famine, especially at the two-year siege of Acre, were very heavy on both sides. Specific events are better attested: about 200 Templars and Hospitallers executed after Hattin, about 2,600–3,000 Muslim prisoners killed at Acre in 1191, and roughly 150 Jews dead at York in 1190, though even these are approximate.

effects: The Second Crusade's failure discredited crusading for a generation and strengthened Nur ad-Din's position.
Saladin's unification of Egypt and Syria and his victory at Hattin ended the first Kingdom of Jerusalem's control of the interior.
The Third Crusade restored a coastal 'second kingdom' of Jerusalem with Acre as capital, which survived for a century.
Cyprus became a Latin kingdom under the Lusignans, lasting until 1489.
The Saladin tithe set a precedent for general taxation for crusades and later for royal taxation.
effectsOnChurch: Crusading was extended formally to Iberia and the Baltic in 1147, diversifying its targets.
Papal theology of crusade as penance was reinforced by explaining defeats as punishment for sin.
Bernard's intervention restated the church's doctrine that Jews must not be killed, but anti-Jewish violence became a recurring accompaniment of crusade preaching, notably in England in 1189–1190.
The military orders gained wealth, castles and influence in the East and in Europe.
Muslim control of Jerusalem from 1187 restricted Latin worship there, while Saladin allowed Eastern Christian clergy to remain at the Holy Sepulchre.
conflicts.legacy: Richard and Saladin became legendary figures of chivalry in both European and Middle Eastern memory, and Saladin's recapture of Jerusalem has been invoked by many modern Arab leaders. The York massacre is commemorated today at Clifford's Tower. The repeated failures of large royal expeditions led to new approaches, including the Fourth Crusade's plan to attack Egypt, which ended at Constantinople instead.

dissenters.name: Bernard of Clairvaux (against anti-Jewish violence)
dissenters.text: While preaching the crusade, Bernard opposed the monk Radulf, writing to the Rhineland clergy that Jews must not be persecuted, killed or driven out, since 'the Jews are for us the living words of Scripture'.

dissenters.name: The Würzburg annalist
dissenters.text: An anonymous chronicler at Würzburg (Annales Herbipolenses) wrote that the Second Crusade was promoted by 'pseudo-prophets, sons of Belial' and that its failure showed God had not approved it, one of the sharpest contemporary criticisms of crusading.

dissenters.name: Ralph Niger
dissenters.text: The English cleric, in De re militari et triplici via peregrinationis Ierosolimitane (c. 1187–1188), questioned whether the recovery of Jerusalem justified killing Muslims, criticised the Saladin tithe and argued that Muslims should be won by preaching rather than the sword.

dissenters.name: Isaac of Stella
dissenters.text: The Cistercian abbot criticised the new military orders as a 'new monstrosity', questioning a form of religious life devoted to killing unbelievers in the name of Christ.

Massacre of the Jews of York (Clifford's Tower)

campaigns.title: Louis VII's march to the East, 1147–1148
campaigns.people: Louis VII, Eleanor of Aquitaine and the French army
campaigns.text: The French marched through Germany and Hungary to Constantinople, followed the Anatolian coast to Ephesus, were mauled at Mount Cadmus beyond Laodicea, sailed from Attalia to Antioch, and joined the council at Acre that chose to besiege Damascus.

campaigns.title: Frederick Barbarossa's crusade, 1189–1190
campaigns.people: Emperor Frederick I and the German army
campaigns.text: Barbarossa's army crossed Hungary and the Balkans, occupied Philippopolis and Adrianople in a dispute with Byzantium, crossed the Hellespont at Gallipoli, stormed Iconium and reached Cilicia, where the emperor drowned.

campaigns.title: Richard I's voyage and campaign, 1190–1192
campaigns.people: Richard I and the Anglo-Norman fleet and army
campaigns.text: Richard set out with Philip II from Vézelay, sailed from Marseille, wintered at Messina, conquered Cyprus, joined the siege of Acre, marched down the coast to victory at Arsuf, and concluded the war at Jaffa.
